name: Sacroiliac joint pain
populations: adults with chronic non-radicular low back pain
summary: A contested source of unilateral low back and buttock pain thought to arise from the sacroiliac joint or its ligaments. Diagnosis rests on a cluster of provocation tests, and the treatment evidence is mixed.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimated at 15–30% of chronic non-radicular low back pain in one review; the estimate is contested because no true gold standard exists

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Three or more of six provocation tests positive: sensitivity 94%, specificity 78% against an anaesthetic block (48 patients); single tests are uninformative

keyFacts.label: Pain pattern
keyFacts.value: Unilateral pain below L5, but referral varies widely; injecting the joint in pain-free volunteers produced pain about 10 cm below and 3 cm lateral to the PSIS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: No imaging finding confirms a painful sacroiliac joint; imaging excludes other causes such as sacroiliitis, fracture or tumour

keyFacts.label: Treatment evidence
keyFacts.value: Mixed: manual therapy 72%, intra-articular steroid 50% and physiotherapy 20% success in a 51-patient trial; radiofrequency gave no clinically important benefit over exercise in the Mint trial

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: Fever, severe pain with inability to weight-bear, night pain, inflammatory back pain or neurological or sphincter change need medical review

overview:
Sacroiliac joint (SIJ) pain is pain thought to arise from the sacroiliac joint or its ligaments, usually felt unilaterally in the low back and buttock below L5. It is estimated to affect 15–30% of people with chronic non-radicular low back pain, but the diagnosis is contested [r1]. No true gold standard exists: the reference test is an anaesthetic block of the joint, and the technique and the relief required have varied widely between studies [r2]. In 85 patients who then had joint blocks, no historical feature, none of 12 SIJ tests and no ensemble of them showed worthwhile diagnostic value [r3].

The best available approach is a cluster of pain provocation tests rather than any single test. Single manual tests of the SIJ were uninformative in a systematic review, but in combination they were informative (positive likelihood ratio 3.2), although changes in probability were small to moderate [r4]. Three or more positive tests out of six had sensitivity 94% and specificity 78% against an anaesthetic block, and when all six fail to provoke familiar pain the SIJ is unlikely to be the source of current back pain [r5]. The thigh thrust test, the compression test and three or more positive tests had discriminative power in pooled data, but the authors cautioned that the tests should be regarded with care because the reference standard is imperfect [r2].

The treatment evidence is mixed. Manual therapy, exercise and taping show benefit in low-quality studies [r6], a small trial favoured manual therapy over physiotherapy and injection for SIJ-related leg pain [r7], and procedural options such as radiofrequency denervation and fusion have both positive and negative trials [r8,r9,r10]. Honest education, a careful screen for other causes and progressive exercise are the foundation, with referral for selected patients whose pain remains disabling.

epidemiology.text: A review estimated that SIJ pain affects between 15 and 30% of people with chronic, non-radicular low back pain. The same review listed predisposing factors (true and apparent leg length discrepancy, older age, inflammatory arthritis, previous spine surgery, pregnancy and trauma) and noted that, compared with facet-mediated and discogenic pain, people with SIJ pain are more likely to report a specific inciting event and unilateral pain below L5. Pain referral patterns are extremely variable [r1]. No population incidence figure was identified in the sources reviewed, and the prevalence estimate depends on the diagnostic criteria used, because no gold standard exists [r2].

intrinsic: True or apparent leg length discrepancy [r1]
Inflammatory arthritis (for example axial spondyloarthritis, which needs separate management) [r1]
Previous lumbar spine surgery, including fusion [r1]
extrinsic: Trauma, including a fall onto the buttock or a sudden jolt through one leg [r1]
Repetitive asymmetrical loading such as running or single-leg sports (plausible association; not tested in the sources reviewed)
Prolonged asymmetrical postures, such as sitting on one side (clinical observation; not tested in the sources reviewed)

mechanism.summary: No single mechanism is established. The sacroiliac joint transfers load between the spine and the legs [r11], and pain is attributed to loading that exceeds the capacity of the joint capsule and ligaments: a sudden jolt or fall, repeated asymmetrical loading, or altered load transfer after pregnancy, spinal surgery or leg length difference [r1]. The joint moves very little: radiostereometric measurement in 22 patients with SIJ pain found very small movements, so the idea of a joint 'out of place' is not well supported [r12].
sequence: A person lands heavily on one leg, falls onto the buttock, twists while lifting, or repeatedly loads one side in a single-leg sport (a specific inciting event is more common than with facet or disc pain) [r1].
Ground force and body weight pass through the pelvis; the sacrum is loaded between the two ilia and the sacroiliac joint transfers the load between spine and legs [r11].
The anterior sacroiliac ligaments and joint capsule are stretched and the joint surfaces are loaded under shear and compression (clinical reasoning).
Capsule, ligaments or the joint itself become the proposed pain source; evidence supports both intra-articular and extra-articular sources [r1].
Pain is felt unilaterally, usually below L5 near the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), and can refer to the buttock, groin or thigh [r1].
Sitting on the affected side, rising from sitting, turning in bed, stairs and single-leg stance reproduce symptoms (clinical observation).
With persistent pain, protective guarding, altered movement and deconditioning of the hip and trunk muscles follow (clinical observation).

variants.name: Traumatic or event-related
variants.description: A fall onto the buttock, a vehicle collision or an awkward single-leg landing; a specific inciting event is more often reported than with facet or disc pain [r1].

variants.name: Insidious or overuse
variants.description: Gradual onset with repeated asymmetrical loading, running or prolonged sitting; many people cannot name a trigger (clinical observation).

variants.name: After lumbar spine surgery or fusion
variants.description: Previous spine surgery is a predisposing factor, possibly from altered load transfer to the sacroiliac joint [r1].

variants.name: Pregnancy-related and post-partum
variants.description: Pregnancy is a predisposing factor [r1]; see the pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain page for the distinct clinical picture.

variants.name: Inflammatory (sacroiliitis)
variants.description: Inflammatory arthritis such as axial spondyloarthritis causes sacroiliac inflammation and is a different disease needing rheumatology review, not mechanical SIJ pain [r1].

anatomy.text: The sacroiliac joints connect the sacrum to the two iliac bones. They are essential for effective load transfer between the spine and the legs, and the sacrum, pelvis and spine are functionally linked by muscle, fascia and ligament [r11]. The joint is synovial in its lower and anterior part, with thin anterior sacroiliac ligaments in front and very strong interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments behind; the sacrotuberous, sacrospinous and iliolumbar ligaments add stability. The joint is inherently stable and moves very little: radiostereometric analysis found only very small movements in patients with SIJ pain, with a self-locking mechanism when the pelvis is loaded in one-leg standing [r12]. The innervation of the joint is variable, which helps explain why referral patterns are so variable [r1].

structures.name: Sacroiliac joint (synovial component) and capsule
structures.role: Joint between sacrum and ilium; transfers load between spine and legs [r11]

structures.name: Anterior sacroiliac ligaments
structures.role: Thin capsular thickening in front of the joint; stretched by load and shear

structures.name: Interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments
structures.role: Very strong ligaments behind the joint that resist sacral nutation and shear; the commonly proposed extra-articular pain sources [r1]

structures.name: Sacrotuberous, sacrospinous and iliolumbar ligaments
structures.role: Add to pelvic stability (force closure); the iliolumbar ligament links L5 to the ilium

structures.name: Gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, multifidus and thoracolumbar fascia
structures.role: Muscular and fascial contributions to force closure across the joint [r11]

structures.name: Pubic symphysis
structures.role: The anterior link in the pelvic ring; it shares load with the sacroiliac joints

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The pain-generating tissue is not established. A review of the evidence supports both intra-articular (joint capsule, cartilage, synovium) and extra-articular (ligament) causes, and clinical studies show benefit from both intra-articular and periarticular steroid injections [r1]. The proposed injury is a load-related overload of the capsule and ligaments, either acute (a fall or jolt) or cumulative, but no imaging or histological feature of a painful joint has been shown to distinguish it from a pain-free one.

Pain mapping in 10 pain-free volunteers who had the joint injected found pain and a zone of hypoaesthesia extending about 10 cm caudally and 3 cm laterally from the PSIS [r13], and clinical referral patterns are extremely variable [r1]. Because physical signs correlate weakly with the response to a diagnostic block [r3], and because the 'positional fault' idea is not supported by movement studies [r12], the practical working model is a mechanically provoked, load-sensitive joint pain with central and behavioural contributors, which the provocation cluster tries to identify.

structures.name: Sacroiliac joint capsule and synovium
structures.effect: Stretched and irritated by load and shear; proposed intra-articular pain source supported by response to intra-articular injection [r1]

structures.name: Anterior sacroiliac ligaments
structures.effect: Stretched under shear and nutation; proposed extra-articular source (clinical reasoning)

structures.name: Interosseous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments
structures.effect: Proposed extra-articular source, targeted by periarticular injection and lateral branch radiofrequency [r1,r10]

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Degenerates with age and in inflammatory arthritis; degeneration is common in people without pain, so imaging change does not prove a pain source (clinical observation)

structures.name: Surrounding structures (gluteal, hip, lumbar)
structures.effect: Common competing pain sources, which is why a careful differential is part of the assessment

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus and medius
muscles.effect: Reduced strength or delayed activation is commonly described with load-related SIJ pain and is a target of rehabilitation; not tested in the sources reviewed

muscles.name: Multifidus and deep abdominals
muscles.effect: Contribute to force closure of the pelvis [r11]; their role in SIJ pain was not tested in the sources reviewed

muscles.name: Piriformis, hamstrings and hip rotators
muscles.effect: Protective tension and tenderness are clinically common and may mimic buttock pain (clinical observation)

muscles.name: Erector spinae and quadratus lumborum
muscles.effect: Reflex guarding on the painful side in the acute phase (clinical observation)

cellular.description: A jolt or sustained asymmetrical load stretches the capsule and sacroiliac ligaments (clinical reasoning).
Capsular and periarticular irritation with synovial inflammation is proposed; both intra-articular and periarticular steroid injection helped in clinical studies [r1].
Ongoing nociceptive input and altered movement patterns can sustain pain, as in other persistent musculoskeletal pain (clinical observation).
Chronic joint degeneration and capsular thickening occur but are not proven to produce pain (clinical observation).

systems.effect: The sacroiliac joint sits between the lumbar spine and hip, so load changes at either site can alter its loading; previous spine surgery and leg length discrepancy are predisposing factors [r1]
The joint's innervation is variable, giving widely variable referral patterns, usually buttock and posterior thigh but sometimes groin or below the knee [r1,r13]
Persistent pain involves central sensitisation and behavioural factors, as in other chronic low back pain (clinical observation)
Pregnancy and post-partum hormonal and mechanical change are predisposing factors; see the pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain page [r1]
Inflammatory arthritis (axial spondyloarthritis) is a predisposing factor and a differential diagnosis needing rheumatology input [r1]
Fear of movement, activity avoidance and poor sleep can maintain pain and disability (clinical observation)

timeframes.summary: No natural-history source was identified for mechanical SIJ pain. Trial follow-up shows the horizons used in practice: 6 and 12 weeks for conservative treatment [r7], 3 months for radiofrequency in the Mint trial [r10], 3 to 9 months for lateral branch neurotomy [r9] and 2 years for fusion [r8].

healing.description: Reassure, modify aggravators and keep moving; many patients are treated for 6 to 12 weeks in conservative trials [r7]
Progressive hip, trunk and pelvic loading, with or without manual therapy, with outcomes assessed at 6 to 12 weeks and 3 months in trials [r7,r10]
Consider diagnostic block, injection or radiofrequency if disabling pain persists despite adequate rehabilitation; benefit from radiofrequency was assessed out to 9 months [r9]
Maintain activity and strength; fusion trials report outcomes at 2 years [r8]

milestones.label: Pain provocation cluster and differential completed
milestones.note: Three or more positive of six tests is the most supported cluster [r5]

milestones.label: First review of response to education and exercise
Outcome review at 6 and 12 weeks
milestones.note: Trial follow-up points for conservative treatment [r7]

milestones.label: Consider referral if disabling pain persists
milestones.note: Clinical convention; Mint participants had to be unresponsive to conservative care [r10]

milestones.label: 2-year outcome in fusion trial
milestones.note: Compared with conservative management in a single, device-company-affiliated RCT [r8]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, typically 4–12 weeks for load-related flares and longer for persistent pain or after a procedure. No validated sacroiliac-specific return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified, so the criteria below are clinical convention.

symptoms: Unilateral low back and buttock pain, typically below L5 and near the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) [r1,r13]
Referral to the buttock, posterior thigh, groin or occasionally below the knee, with extremely variable patterns [r1]
A specific inciting event (fall, jolt, awkward lift or landing) is reported more often than with facet or disc pain [r1]
Aggravation by sitting on the affected side, rising from sitting, stairs, turning in bed, single-leg stance and prolonged standing (clinical observation)
Pain reproduced by the familiar movement, with no neurological symptoms (no dermatomal pain or numbness)
signs: Tenderness over the PSIS or sacral sulcus on the painful side (nonspecific)
Reproduction of familiar pain by one or more provocation tests; a cluster of three or more positive tests is more informative than any single test [r5,r2]
Antalgic gait or reduced single-leg stance tolerance (clinical observation)
Normal neurological examination and no neural tension signs
Lumbar movements and hip examination usually do not reproduce the pain, which helps exclude those sources

subjective: Pain site: unilateral below L5 near the PSIS, with referral to the buttock, thigh or groin [r1]
Onset: a specific event (fall, jolt, awkward landing or lift), pregnancy, previous spine surgery or insidious [r1]
Aggravating and easing factors: sitting on one side, rising from sitting, stairs, turning in bed, single-leg stance and running
Red flags: fever, night or constant pain, weight loss, history of cancer, steroid use, IV drug use, recent infection, trauma
Inflammatory features: age under 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise but not with rest (clinical convention)
Neurological and sphincter symptoms: leg weakness, saddle numbness, bladder, bowel and sexual function
Leg length difference, previous surgery or hip problems, sport and training load, work posture and goals
observation: Standing and sitting posture, pelvic asymmetry and trunk lean (positional asymmetries correlate poorly with pain; do not over-interpret) [r12]
Gait: antalgic pattern or reduced stance time on the painful side
Single-leg stance: pelvic drop or trunk compensation
palpation: Tenderness at the PSIS and long posterior sacroiliac ligament (nonspecific)
Gluteal, piriformis and lumbar paraspinal tenderness to screen competing sources
Greater trochanter tenderness (gluteal tendinopathy) and pubic symphysis tenderness
rangeOfMotion: Active lumbar movements: usually pain-free or non-provocative, which helps exclude a lumbar source
Hip range of motion, especially flexion with adduction (FADIR) and internal and external rotation, to exclude hip pathology
Repeated movements and sustained postures to screen for a lumbar directional preference
strength: Hip abductors, extensors and external rotators; single-leg bridge and calf raise repetitions
Trunk endurance: side plank and prone hold
Resisted hip movements for gluteal tendon pain
neuro: Lower limb myotomes, dermatomes and reflexes: normal in SIJ pain
Straight leg raise and slump to screen for lumbar radiculopathy
Saddle sensation and bladder, bowel and sexual function screen when symptoms are bilateral or progressive
functional: Single-leg stance and single-leg squat quality
Sport- or work-specific tasks that reproduce the pain

specialTests.name: Cluster of SIJ pain provocation tests (three or more positive of six)
specialTests.purpose: Identify the SIJ as a likely source of familiar pain
specialTests.procedure: Perform the provocation tests (commonly distraction, compression, thigh thrust, sacral thrust and Gaenslen's on each side); record whether each reproduces the patient's familiar pain.
specialTests.positive: Three or more of six tests reproduce familiar pain. When none of the six does, the SIJ is unlikely to be the source of current back pain [r5].
specialTests.sensitivity: 94% (three or more of six tests; 48 patients; reference: anaesthetic block)
specialTests.specificity: 78% (three or more of six tests; 48 patients; reference: anaesthetic block)

specialTests.name: Thigh thrust (posterior shear) test
specialTests.purpose: Stress the SIJ with a posterior-directed shear
specialTests.procedure: Supine, hip flexed to about 90°, apply a posterior force through the femur along its long axis while stabilising the pelvis.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain in the buttock or SIJ region. Pooled diagnostic odds ratio 18.461 (95% CI 5.82–58.53) against double infiltration [r2].

specialTests.name: Compression test
specialTests.purpose: Compress the SIJs with side-lying downward force on the iliac crest
specialTests.procedure: Side-lying with the painful side up, hips flexed, apply downward pressure through the iliac crest.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain. Pooled diagnostic odds ratio 3.88 (95% CI 1.7–8.9) [r2].

specialTests.name: Three or more positive stressing tests (pooled composite)
specialTests.purpose: Increase the probability that the SIJ is the pain source
specialTests.procedure: Perform several stressing tests and count the positives.
specialTests.positive: Three or more positive. Pooled diagnostic odds ratio 17.16 (95% CI 7.6–39) [r2]. Combined manual tests had a positive likelihood ratio of 3.2 (95% CI 2.3–4.4) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.29 [r4].

specialTests.name: Distraction (gapping), sacral thrust and Gaenslen's tests
specialTests.purpose: Further stress tests commonly included in the cluster
specialTests.procedure: Distraction: supine, apply posteriorly directed force to both ASISs. Sacral thrust: prone, apply anterior pressure on the sacrum. Gaenslen's: supine at the edge of the plinth, hip flexed with the other leg extended off the plinth.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain. Single manual tests were uninformative in a systematic review, and no pooled accuracy figures for these individual tests were identified in the sources reviewed [r4].

specialTests.name: Standing hip flexion (Gillet) test and other motion tests
specialTests.purpose: Historically used to assess SIJ motion
specialTests.procedure: Standing, the patient flexes one hip while the examiner palpates the PSIS and sacrum.
specialTests.positive: Not recommended as a diagnostic tool. In 22 patients with SIJ pain, radiostereometric analysis registered very small movements, so the test cannot be recommended to evaluate joint motion [r12].

clinicalRules.name: Laslett provocation cluster
clinicalRules.description: Three or more positive out of six pain provocation tests, or any two of four selected tests, had the best predictive power against intra-articular anaesthetic block; when all six tests are negative the SIJ is unlikely to be the source of current back pain. The reference standard is itself imperfect [r5,r2].

clinicalRules.name: Exclude the lumbar spine and hip first
clinicalRules.description: SIJ pain is a diagnosis made after reasonable exclusion of lumbar, hip and neural sources, because no history feature or single test is reliable [r3,r1].

clinicalRules.name: Red flag screen
clinicalRules.description: Fever, severe pain with inability to weight-bear, night or constant pain, inflammatory back pain features, cauda equina symptoms or a history of cancer need medical assessment before treating a presumed SIJ source (see red flags).

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric Pain Rating Scale (0–10) for pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the Mint radiofrequency trials; the prespecified minimal clinically important difference was 2 points [r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Disability outcome in the fusion trial and the sham-controlled neurotomy trial [r8,r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Specific Functional Scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Individual goals such as sitting at work, running or climbing stairs

outcomeMeasures.name: SF-36 bodily pain and physical function
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in the sham-controlled neurotomy trial [r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg stance and single-leg squat quality, with a pain provocation re-test
outcomeMeasures.use: Track change in the provocation cluster and function

imaging.indication: Trauma, suspected fracture or arthritis, and as a screen before other imaging
imaging.findings: Sacroiliac joint space and sclerosis, pubic symphysis alignment and hip disease; they do not identify a painful SIJ (clinical convention)

imaging.modality: MRI of the sacroiliac joints (with STIR)
imaging.indication: Suspected sacroiliitis (inflammatory back pain or axial spondyloarthritis), stress fracture, infection or tumour
imaging.findings: Bone marrow oedema, erosions, effusion or fracture. These exclude other diagnoses; no imaging finding was identified in the sources reviewed that confirms mechanical SIJ pain, and joint degeneration may be seen without pain (clinical observation).

imaging.indication: Bony detail after trauma or before procedures; suspected sacral fracture
imaging.findings: Joint degeneration, sclerosis, fracture or fusion

imaging.modality: Fluoroscopically guided diagnostic sacroiliac joint block
imaging.indication: Used by pain physicians to confirm the SIJ as the source before procedures; not a physiotherapy test
imaging.findings: Pain relief after local anaesthetic; there is no gold standard, and technique and required relief vary [r2,r3]

differentials.name: Lumbar facet joint pain
differentials.distinguishing: Central or paraspinal pain above L5, extension-related, with SIJ provocation tests negative; single tests for facet joint pain were uninformative and single SIJ tests were also uninformative, so the two are not reliably separated by any one test [r4].

differentials.name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Dermatomal leg pain, positive neural tension and neurological signs; SIJ pain does not follow a dermatome.

differentials.name: Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain during or after pregnancy involving the pelvic girdle, with a different assessment cluster and management; see that page.

differentials.name: Sacral stress or insufficiency fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual onset in runners or older adults with low bone density; pain on weight-bearing and hopping; MRI shows marrow oedema or a fracture line.

differentials.name: Deep gluteal syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Buttock pain with sitting, tenderness near the sciatic notch and piriformis tests positive, without a positive SIJ cluster.

differentials.name: Gluteal tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Lateral hip pain with palpation at the greater trochanter, side-lying and single-leg stance pain, and a negative SIJ cluster.

differentials.name: Hip joint pathology (femoroacetabular impingement, labral tear, osteoarthritis)
differentials.distinguishing: Groin pain, restricted and painful hip flexion and internal rotation, positive FADIR; groin referral can mimic SIJ pain.

differentials.name: Coccydynia
differentials.distinguishing: Midline pain at the coccyx that is worse sitting and rising, with local tenderness.

differentials.name: Axial spondyloarthritis (sacroiliitis)
differentials.distinguishing: Younger adults with insidious onset, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise not rest, alternating buttock pain; MRI shows inflammation. Needs rheumatology review [r1].

redFlags: EMERGENCY: possible cauda equina syndrome. New urinary retention or loss of bladder sensation, faecal incontinence, saddle (perineal) numbness, new sexual dysfunction or bilateral leg weakness need same-day emergency referral (see the cauda equina syndrome page).
Fever, severe pain with inability to weight-bear, recent infection, IV drug use or immunosuppression: consider septic sacroiliitis and arrange urgent medical assessment.
Constant or night pain, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer or significant trauma: consider tumour or fracture and arrange imaging and medical review.

Inflammatory back pain features (age under 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, alternating buttock pain): refer for rheumatology assessment, as sacroiliitis is a different disease needing different management [r1].
Sacral insufficiency fracture risk (older adult, osteoporosis, long-term steroids, sudden weight-bearing pain): arrange imaging and protect weight-bearing until clarified.
Progressive neurological deficit or radicular pain: examine and refer for lumbar spine assessment rather than attributing the pain to the SIJ [r3].

management.principles: Because the diagnosis is contested, start with a careful exclusion of other causes, explain honestly that the SIJ is a plausible but unproven source, and treat with education, activity and a progressive exercise program, adding manual therapy for symptom relief. Treatment evidence is mixed and mostly low quality: physiotherapy interventions (manipulation, exercise and taping) were effective in low-to-average quality studies [r6], a small trial favoured manual therapy [r7], injections showed intermediate-term benefit in clinical studies [r1], and procedural options have conflicting trials [r8,r9,r10]. Reserve injection, radiofrequency denervation and fusion for patients with persistent disabling pain, a positive provocation cluster and failure of well-delivered conservative care, and discuss the limits of the evidence.

medical.name: Intra-articular or periarticular corticosteroid injection
medical.description: A review found that clinical studies demonstrate intermediate-term benefit for both intra- and extra-articular steroid injections [r1]. In a small randomised trial of 51 patients with SIJ-related leg pain, intra-articular injection succeeded in 9 of 18 patients (50%) [r7]. The evidence is mostly small and uncontrolled.

medical.name: Radiofrequency denervation (lateral branch neurotomy)
medical.description: Evidence conflicts. In a sham-controlled trial of 51 patients with a positive response to dual lateral branch blocks, 47% of treated patients and 12% of sham patients achieved success at 3 months, with benefit in 38% and 59% at 6 and 9 months [r9]. In the Mint sacroiliac joint trial (228 participants), radiofrequency added to an exercise program gave a 3-month pain difference of −0.71 on a 0–10 scale (95% CI −1.35 to −0.06), below the prespecified 2-point minimal clinically important difference, and the authors concluded that the findings do not support radiofrequency denervation [r10]. A review states that radiofrequency may provide relief lasting up to 1 year in those without sustained relief from injections [r1].

medical.name: Minimally invasive sacroiliac joint arthrodesis
medical.description: In a randomised trial of 103 adults, 2-year low back pain improved by 45 points after arthrodesis and 11 points after conservative management (difference 34 points), and the ODI improved by 26 versus 8 points. Patients could not be blinded to surgery versus conservative care, the authors included employees of the device company, and 39 severe adverse events occurred after arthrodesis (including nerve impingement and a gluteal haematoma) [r8]. Only for selected patients with refractory pain.

medical.name: Repeated injections or procedures without an exit plan
medical.description: Repeated procedures do not address the load, movement and behavioural contributors and the evidence for repeated treatment is lacking in the sources reviewed (clinical convention).

physio.name: Education, reassurance and activity advice
physio.description: Explain that the joint is a plausible source of load-related pain but that this is not proven, that movements are small and the joint is not 'out of place', and that staying active within limits helps. Treat the person rather than a label [r12,r1].

physio.name: Manual therapy (manipulation or mobilisation)
physio.description: In a single-blinded trial of 51 patients with SIJ-related leg pain, manual therapy succeeded in 13 of 18 (72%) compared with 3 of 15 (20%) for physiotherapy and 9 of 18 (50%) for intra-articular injection (p = 0.01) at 6 and 12 weeks [r7]. In a systematic review, manipulation was the most effective approach in studies of low to average quality [r6].

physio.name: Progressive exercise therapy (hip, trunk and pelvic strengthening)
physio.description: A systematic review of 9 low- to average-quality studies included 3 on exercise and reported reductions in pain and disability [r6]. Exercise was the standard comparator in the Mint radiofrequency trials [r10]. Dosages are clinical convention.

physio.name: Kinesio taping
physio.description: Three taping studies of low to average quality in the same review reported benefit for pain, disability and pelvic asymmetry [r6].

physio.name: Motion palpation and positional-fault correction to select or direct treatment
physio.description: The standing hip flexion test cannot be recommended as a diagnostic test, because only very small movements occur in the sacroiliac joints [r12]. Do not base treatment on a presumed 'upslip', 'rotation' or 'out-of-place' joint (clinical convention).

physio.name: Screening for competing and associated sources
physio.description: Since no test is definitive, screen for lumbar, hip, gluteal and neural sources and review the provocation cluster at follow-up [r3,r5].

education: Your pain may be coming from the sacroiliac joint, which sits at the base of the spine on each side. We cannot prove it, because no single test or scan can, but the pattern of your pain and a group of tests make it a reasonable explanation.
The sacroiliac joint moves very little, and it is not 'out of place' or locked. Treatment aims to settle pain and rebuild strength and confidence, not to click anything back.
Staying active is part of treatment. Short walks, strengthening for the hips and trunk, and avoiding long spells in one position usually help.
Some people benefit from manual therapy, taping or an injection as a stepping stone to exercise. Evidence for each is modest, and we will review what is working.
If pain stays disabling after good rehabilitation, specialist options exist, but their evidence is mixed and each has risks.

Go to an emergency department the same day if you develop numbness around the genitals or buttocks, difficulty passing urine, loss of bowel control, fever with severe pain, or leg weakness that is getting worse.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is criteria-based. The evidence supports exercise as a component of care but does not define a program, so dosages are clinical convention [r6,r10]. Settle pain with education and non-provocative movement, restore pelvic and hip control, then build strength and single-leg capacity, then return to sport or work with graded asymmetrical loading. Manual therapy can be used for short-term relief to enable exercise [r7]. Re-test the provocation cluster at each review. Pain that is not responding, or any red flag, needs medical review.

stages.name: Settle & load-manage
goals: Understand the diagnosis and its uncertainty
Reduce provocation: avoid sitting on one side, prolonged single-leg stance and sudden asymmetrical loading
Complete the red flag and differential screen
precautions: Same-day referral for any cauda equina features
Avoid forceful end-range or asymmetrical stretching of the painful side early
Review any fever, night pain or inflammatory features before progressing

exercises.name: Walking in short, regular bouts
exercises.dosage: 5–15 minutes, 3–5 times daily, as symptoms allow (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Even steps, relaxed arm swing; stop before pain builds

exercises.name: Supine knee to chest (both legs, gentle)
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 20–30 seconds, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Relax into the floor; keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Gentle isometric glute squeeze in supine
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions of 5-second holds, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Squeeze gently; do not provoke familiar pain

exercises.name: Deep abdominal activation with breathing
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions of 5-second holds, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Gentle co-contraction, continue breathing

exercises.name: Position changes
exercises.dosage: Change position every 30–45 minutes while sitting; sit evenly on both sit bones (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Avoid crossing the legs or sitting on one side

progressionCriteria: Resting pain 4/10 or less and sleep not routinely disturbed
Red flag and differential screen completed
Understands the plan and the aggravating positions to modify

stages.name: Restore pelvic & hip control
goals: Hip and trunk control in neutral and light loading
precautions: Progress a new demand only if pain is 2/10 or lower and settles within 24 hours (clinical convention)
Keep the pelvis level; avoid aggravating asymmetrical stretches

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 10 repetitions with a 3-second hold, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; ribs down; keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Side-lying clamshell
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 12 repetitions per side, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Roll from the hip, not the back; keep feet together

exercises.name: Bird-dog
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side with 5-second holds, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Reach long; keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Dead bug
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per side, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Low back flat; slow, controlled limb movement

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 30 seconds per leg, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Level pelvis; no trunk lean

progressionCriteria: Pain 2/10 or lower during exercises and daily tasks
Single-leg stance 30 seconds each side without pelvic drop

stages.name: Build strength & single-leg capacity
precautions: Increase load or volume by about 5–10% a week, one variable at a time (clinical convention)
Hold back if familiar pain returns or lasts into the next day

exercises.name: Hip thrust
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions at a load leaving 2–3 in reserve, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Tuck the pelvis at the top; keep the pelvis level

exercises.name: Single-leg bridge
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per leg, 3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level; avoid rotation

exercises.name: Side plank (knees, then feet)
exercises.dosage: 3 holds of 15–30 seconds per side, building to 45 seconds (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Stack the hips; lift the waist away from the floor

exercises.name: Split squat
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8 repetitions per leg, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Knee tracks over the toes; trunk upright; level pelvis

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions, progressive load, 2 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Hinge from the hips; keep the bar close

progressionCriteria: No familiar pain with loaded single-leg exercise
Side plank at least 30 seconds each side and symmetry within about 10% (clinical convention)
Provocation cluster negative or markedly reduced on re-test

stages.name: Return to sport & work
goals: Meet the physical demands of work or sport
Graded asymmetrical loading (running, change of direction, single-leg sport)
precautions: Build running and single-leg loading in steps of about 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
Step back one level if pain returns for more than 24 hours
Review if pain plateaus; consider referral for procedural options only after adequate rehabilitation

exercises.name: Step-up
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–10 repetitions per leg, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Lead with the hip; control the descent

exercises.name: Single-leg squat
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions per leg (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Control the knee and pelvis

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate 2 minutes running and 2 minutes walking, building toward continuous running over 4–6 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Short, quick steps; level pelvis

exercises.name: Hop and landing progressions
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 6–8 repetitions per leg (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Soft landing; level pelvis

exercises.name: Sport- or work-specific tasks
exercises.dosage: Start at 50% of usual volume and build weekly (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality over volume

progressionCriteria: Full training or duties completed without familiar pain

criteria: No validated sacroiliac-specific return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
Pain-free daily activities and sport or work tasks, with no pain the following day
Provocation cluster negative or markedly reduced on repeat testing
Single-leg stance, squat and hop quality symmetrical, with strength within about 10% side to side
Able to run or perform sport-specific asymmetrical loading at the required volume without pain
Self-management and flare-up plan in place
tests: Repeat the SIJ provocation cluster and compare with baseline [r5]
Single-leg squat, single-leg bridge and hop quality
Side plank and trunk endurance, both sides
Run or sport drill at full speed
Oswestry Disability Index or Patient-Specific Functional Scale against the person's goal

prognosis: No natural-history estimate for mechanical SIJ pain was identified in the sources reviewed, and outcomes depend on treatment. In a small single-blinded trial of 51 patients with SIJ-related leg pain, 56% were treated successfully at 6 to 12 weeks, with manual therapy succeeding in 72%, injection in 50% and physiotherapy in 20% [r7]. A review reported that radiofrequency denervation may give relief lasting up to 1 year in those without sustained relief from injections [r1]; in a sham-controlled trial, 59% of treated patients had success at 9 months [r9], while in the Mint SIJ trial the 3-month effect of radiofrequency added to exercise was below the minimal clinically important difference [r10]. In the fusion trial, pain improved by 45 points after arthrodesis compared with 11 points after conservative management at 2 years, but patients could not be blinded, the authors included employees of the device company, and conservative-arm patients who crossed over to surgery improved [r8]. All of these results sit on a contested diagnosis with an imperfect reference standard [r2].
prevention: No intervention has been shown to prevent SIJ pain; the points below are clinical convention.
Maintain hip and trunk strength and general fitness, and build running and single-leg loading gradually.
Address leg length difference or hip stiffness when clinically relevant (true or apparent leg length discrepancy is a predisposing factor) [r1].
Return progressively after pregnancy or lumbar surgery, and treat early back and buttock pain with activity and education rather than rest.
clinicalPearls: Use the cluster, never a single test. Single manual tests were uninformative, whereas three or more positives of six had sensitivity 94% and specificity 78%, and six negatives rule the joint out as the current source [r4,r5].

Remember the reference standard is imperfect. The anaesthetic block has no gold-standard technique, so test accuracy is only as good as the block [r2], and in one study no historical feature or ensemble of 12 tests was valuable [r3].
Pain below L5, unilateral, with a specific event is the typical pattern, but referral is extremely variable and the volunteer map centres about 10 cm below and 3 cm lateral to the PSIS [r1,r13].
Do not treat the pelvis as a joint that goes 'out'. Only very small movements occur, and the standing hip flexion test cannot be recommended [r12].
Screen for sacroiliitis and other mimics. Inflammatory back pain in a young adult is a rheumatology problem, and a stress fracture in a runner or an older adult needs imaging [r1].
Be candid about procedures. Radiofrequency and fusion trials conflict or have limitations, and a first-line rehabilitation program should come first [r8,r9,r10].

animation.title: How sacroiliac joint pain can develop

captions.text: An active adult steps down awkwardly onto one leg, or lands heavily on hard ground.
A sudden, unbalanced load travels up the leg and across one side of the pelvis.
Pain follows on one side of the lower back and buttock, often near the PSIS.
The cause is not certain, and no single test or scan can prove the joint is the source.
Zooming into the pelvis from the front, to see the sacroiliac joint where the sacrum meets the ilium.
The sacroiliac joint links the sacrum to the ilium and transfers load between the spine and the leg.
Body weight pushes down through the sacrum while ground force pushes up through the ilium.
A sudden or repeated asymmetrical load stretches the joint capsule and its ligaments.
The capsule and ligaments can become irritated and inflamed.
Pain is felt on one side, below L5, near the back of the pelvis.
It is unproven which tissue hurts, and a scan cannot confirm that the joint is the source.
A healthy joint capsule: a smooth synovial lining and organised collagen.
Overload can inflame the lining and the capsule around it.
Persistent irritation can thicken and stiffen the capsule with fibrous tissue.
Over years the tissue remodels. Which tissue generates pain remains unproven.
